what: Marian Rejewski's 'bomba kryptologiczna', an electrically driven aggregate of six Enigma machines at the Polish Cipher Bureau, designed about October 1938 and ready in mid-November 1938.

sources.title: Bomba (cryptography)
sources.quote: In mid-November 1938, the bombs were ready, and the reconstructing of daily keys now took about two hours.

sources.title: Bomba (cryptography)
sources.quote: invented the "bomba kryptologiczna" (cryptologic bomb), probably in October 1938

note: Earlier candidate: the Polish cyclometer (designed 'probably in 1934 or 1935'), which catalogued cycle structures of Enigma permutations to speed decryption. Rejected as the first because it prepared a catalogue rather than testing keys itself, though it arguably also fits 'analysing patterns'. The British Bombe (1940), Heath Robinson (1943) and Colossus (Mark 1 first attacked a message on 5 February 1944) are later; the first pass named Colossus. Before 1938 the Poles used hand 'grill' methods. Pre-electromechanical cryptanalytic machines (e.g. punched-card tabulator aids in the 1930s) were not checked.

what: Thomas Sutton photographed a tartan ribbon through red, green and blue filters for James Clerk Maxwell's 1861 lecture; the three images projected together gave a full-color picture.
fit: Natural colors were recorded photographically without hand-tinting, by the three-color method.

sources.title: Color photography
sources.quote: with the first color photograph produced by Thomas Sutton for a Maxwell lecture in 1861

note: Earlier direct-color attempts: Edmond Becquerel (1848-51) and Niepce de Saint-Victor recorded colors on silver plates but the colors could not be fixed and faded in light, and Levi Hill's Hillotype (about 1850) was unreliable (Wikipedia). Seebeck's 1810 colors on silver chloride were spectrum effects. These are rejected as non-lasting, but a stricter reading could date the first demonstration to 1848-1850.
searched: Wikipedia Color photography; archive.org search for Maxwell/Sutton 1861 (no usable hit).

fit: A volumetric display, not a hologram: a swept-screen CRT that draws changing points in a real 3-D volume seen in a viewing globe, so the picture is a true volumetric one rather than a stereo pair; the definition's 'holographic' wording is only its label.

Candidates rejected: Parker/Wallis 'Three-dimensional cathode-ray tube displays' (IEE 1948) and MacKay's 'projective' displays (1949) only rotate a 3-D plot into a 2-D view, no volumetric picture; the 1962 optical holograms and Cross's 1972 multiplex hologram are static or fixed-sequence recordings; Traub's varifocal-mirror display (Applied Optics, 1967-06) and ITT's rotating-screen air-traffic display (Aviation Week 1960-10-31, 'gives 3-D effect from any viewing angle without need for stereoscopic illusion', working small-scale model) are later but clearly fit. Earlier volumetric proposals exist (1912 postulate) but no working device was found before Withey's.

what: Gemini III (Grissom and Young) flew with the IBM-built Gemini onboard digital computer, which navigated and produced reentry guidance commands for the crew.

note: Kept the second pass date (Gemini III, 23 March 1965, first crewed flight of the IBM Gemini guidance computer), now with a fetched contemporary press kit and a 1967 NASA summary. Gemini III's lift shortfall meant the crew did not follow the computer all the way, and the full onboard-computer rendezvous burns came on Gemini 6A/7 (Dec 1965); Gemini 4 (June 1965) could not use the computer for reentry after a memory alteration. Earlier candidates rejected: Mercury (1961-63; no onboard digital computer, orbits computed by ground IBM 7090s), Vostok (analog 'Globus' navigation), Atlas/Titan/Thor launch-vehicle guidance computers (1958-62) and Saturn I (1964), which steer rockets or missiles rather than a spacecraft and were mostly ground-based or not checked; submarine and ship inertial navigators (1950s, analog, no burns). The press kit only shows that a spacecraft computer existed and was loaded for the flight; the claim that it flew on Gemini III rests on the 1967 summary. Practical use is given as the same flight: it was a real mission, not a bench test, but a full 'real purpose' use (rendezvous) was Dec 1965.

what: Thirion, Duchesnay, Hubbard, Dubois, Poline, Lebihan and Dehaene (NeuroSpin, France) decoded fMRI activity to reconstruct the visual pattern that subjects were only imagining, using inverse retinotopy and supervised classifiers (NeuroImage 33(4), 2006).
fit: From brain activity alone, the machine reconstructed an image the person was holding in mind (a mental image, not a displayed stimulus), shown as a reconstructed pattern; the images were crude flickering-pattern shapes.

sources.title: Inverse retinotopy: Inferring the visual content of images from brain activation patterns
sources.quote: in five data sets, our algorithms could reconstruct and predict with significant accuracy a pattern imagined by the subjects

review3: An earlier strict fit than the 2025 'mind captioning' paper: a 2023 decoder wrote out as text what people silently imagined saying.
check_note: Replaces Tang et al. 2023. The definition covers text of thoughts OR mental images/dreams on a screen. Thirion 2006 reconstructs an imagined pattern from fMRI, earlier than the 2023 language decoder; it is crude (a self-chosen pattern from a small set of flickering stimuli), so confidence is low. Rejected as earlier candidates: Farwell and Donchin 1988 P300 speller and Birbaumer 1999 slow-cortical-potential speller (the user picks letters by attention or cursor control; this is selection, not reading out thought content); Vidal 1973 (cursor); Miyawaki 2008 and Nishimoto 2011 (reconstruct images being viewed, not mental images); Horikawa 2013 dream decoding (word categories only); Willett 2021 and Moses 2021 (attempted handwriting or speech); Makin 2020 (spoken sentences). Tang 2023 (PMC11304553, FOUND) is the first decoder of open-ended silent thought into word sequences, the best fit if the checker prefers the text reading of the definition.

what: Hideo Kodama (Nagoya Municipal Industrial Research Institute) built three machines that fabricated solid plastic models by exposing liquid photo-hardening polymer to UV light and stacking the solidified cross-sections; his papers appeared in 1981.
fit: An automatic machine built a solid object layer by layer by solidifying material cross-section by cross-section (mask or scanning-fibre exposure, an XYZ plotter), though whether the layers came from a digital design file is not stated.

sources.title: Automatic method for fabricating a three-dimensional plastic model with photo-hardening polymer
sources.quote: A solid model is fabricated by exposing liquid photo-hardening polymer to ultraviolet rays, and stacking the cross-sectional solidified layers.

sources.title: 3D printing
sources.quote: He filed a patent for this XYZ plotter, which was published on 10 November 1981.

note: Same event as the second pass, now with Kodama's own 1981 paper (abstract) as contemporary source; the date is 1981 only (Wikipedia gives April for the first paper and the apparatus work as April 1980; the Review of Scientific Instruments paper is November 1981). The paper itself says the operation 'can be easily automated', so full automation from a digital design is not certain; if that is judged essential, the next fit is Chuck Hull's first stereolithography part (1983, CAD-driven; patent 1984, granted 1986), which I did not source. Earlier candidates rejected: Willème's photosculpture (1860, not layered additive from a design), Swainson / Ciraud / Housholder patents of 1971-79 (patents, no demonstration), Raytheon 1982 powder patent (later).
searched: Crossref for Kodama (abstract), Wikipedia 3D printing and Stereolithography, ia_search3 stereolithography 1986-90; patents only seen via Wikipedia.

what: 3D Systems announced its stereolithography system (laser-cured acrylic resin, computer-controlled platform) as a product letting architects make detailed building models in minutes (Progressive Architecture, May 1987).
fit: A commercial machine built solid models automatically from computer sections of a design, layer by layer in photo-curing resin, for real design work.

sources.title: New Products: Model-building Electronically (3D Systems, Inc.)

sources.title: Stereolithography

note: Second pass had 1987 from memory (SLA-1) with a Wikipedia source that only supports commercialisation after 1986; now confirmed by a 1987 trade-press product notice. Earlier internal use at Hull's firm (1983-86) and any earlier lab use of Kodama's machine were not documented as outside-the-lab service.
searched: ia_search3 'stereolithography 3D Systems Hull' 1987-90 and 'stereolithography laser resin' 1986-88; Progressive Architecture May 1987 read.

what: Ivan Sutherland and students built a head-mounted display whose computer generated a stereo perspective view that changed as the wearer moved his head (running on a PDP-1 at Harvard in August 1968).
fit: A computer draws a three-dimensional world in each eye and updates it from head tracking so the user sees it as if it were around him, though only as crude wireframe lines.

sources.publisher: Harvard University / ARPA report (Computer History Museum archive)

Rejected earlier: Heilig's Sensorama (1962 prototype, pre-filmed, not computer-generated), Philco Headsight (1961, camera-fed remote viewing), Sutherland's 1965 'Ultimate Display' (a proposal).
